$schema: Capability graph for hal-plus scenario generation. See LLM_HALPLUS_V2.md §10.2.

capabilities.label: Terraform Enterprise
capabilities.provides: A self-hosted Terraform Enterprise runtime (org/project/workspaces, remote runs).

observable.what: The TFE web UI is reachable and the bootstrap org/project exist.

capabilities.notes: Primary target = container hal-tfe at https://tfe.localhost:8443, org hal, project Dave.

capabilities.label: GitLab CE (lab VCS host)
capabilities.provides: A local GitLab CE instance hosting the demo repo that TFE links to via VCS.

observable.what: The GitLab project (root/tfe-agent-demo) is reachable with main.tf + .gitlab-ci.yml seeded.

capabilities.notes: Bootstrapped as a side effect of the vcs-workflow command; not a standalone hal product. GitLab CE 18.10.1 at http://127.0.0.1:8080, login root / hal9000FTW.

capabilities.label: Terraform VCS-driven workflow
capabilities.provides: VCS-driven auto-apply of Terraform runs: a commit to the GitLab repo triggers a TFE run.
capabilities.manualTrigger: Push a commit to the main branch of the GitLab repo (root/tfe-agent-demo).

observable.what: GitLab fires a webhook to TFE, which queues and auto-applies a run; the latest run appears at the top of the workspace runs page.

capabilities.notes: Workspace auto-apply + execution-mode remote + queue-all-runs + vcs-repo linked on branch main. Twin target uses -bis names. See LLM_HALPLUS_V2.md §9.

capabilities.label: Terraform API/CLI-driven workflow
capabilities.provides: An ephemeral TFX API helper shell to drive TFE runs via the API/CLI instead of a VCS repo.
capabilities.manualTrigger: From the helper shell, drive workspaces and queue runs with tfx / the TFE API.

observable.what: Runs appear in the TFE workspace, queued via the API/CLI rather than a VCS webhook.

capabilities.notes: Builds/runs the ephemeral helper container hal-tfe-api (image hal-tfe-api:latest, base ghcr.io/straubt1/tfx:latest) and drops into a shell. Alias: api. statusTool shares its handler with get_tfe_cli_status and returns TEXT status (no structured payload) -> observable.linkFrom is null; the tfe.* dotted paths in access come from the dependsOn tfe node's get_tfe_status.

capabilities.label: HashiCorp Vault
capabilities.provides: A running Vault instance (secrets engines, auth methods, policies).

observable.what: The Vault API is reachable and unsealed.

capabilities.notes: Container hal-vault; root token surfaced by the CLI. statusTool returns TEXT status (not a structured payload), so no dotted-path linkFrom.

capabilities.label: Vault dynamic database credentials
capabilities.provides: On-demand, short-lived database credentials minted by Vault (no static DB passwords).
capabilities.manualTrigger: Request a credential: vault read database/creds/dba-role

observable.what: Vault mints a just-in-time MariaDB username/password with a 2m default TTL (max 2h) that auto-revokes when the lease expires.

capabilities.notes: MariaDB container hal-vault-mariadb at mariadb.localhost:3306. Vault mounts database/ (mysql-database-plugin), rotates the vaultadmin root password, role dba-role default_ttl 2m / max_ttl 2h, revocation DROP USER. statusTool returns TEXT status (no structured payload).

capabilities.label: HashiCorp Boundary
capabilities.provides: A running Boundary controller/worker that brokers identity-based, least-exposure access to targets without distributing network or credential details to users.

observable.what: The Boundary controller API is reachable and the admin console responds.

capabilities.notes: Container hal-boundary; admin/controller API at http://boundary.localhost:9200. statusTool returns TEXT status (no structured payload), so no dotted-path linkFrom.

capabilities.label: Boundary brokered database access (Vault dynamic credentials)
capabilities.provides: Identity-based access to a MariaDB target where Boundary brokers short-lived credentials minted on demand by Vault's database secrets engine — the user authenticates as themselves and never sees a database password.
capabilities.manualTrigger: Authenticate to Boundary as dba-user, then open a brokered session to the target: (1) BOUNDARY_AUTHENTICATE_PASSWORD_PASSWORD=password boundary authenticate password -addr http://boundary.localhost:9200 -auth-method-id <lab-auth> -login-name dba-user, then (2) boundary connect mysql -addr http://boundary.localhost:9200 -target-id <mariadb-secure-access>.

observable.what: Boundary opens a session to the mariadb-secure-access target and injects a fresh, Vault-minted MySQL credential (role dba-role) into the connection. The credential is short-lived and auto-revokes when the Vault lease expires; no static database password is handed to the user.

capabilities.notes: Requires `hal vault database enable` first (provides container hal-vault-mariadb + Vault role database/creds/dba-role). The --with-vault path attaches Boundary to the existing hal-vault-mariadb and runs linkBoundaryToVault(): writes Vault policy boundary-controller, mints an orphan 24h token, then in Boundary creates credential store hal-vault-store (type vault, address http://hal-vault:8200), credential library mariadb-dba-creds (type vault-generic, path database/creds/dba-role, http_method GET) and adds it as the brokered credential source on target mariadb-secure-access. Boundary scopes: org hal-academy / project db-infrastructure. Auth method lab-auth (password), account login dba-user / password, principal user 'DBA Admin', role dba-role. Target type tcp, default_port 3306, host mariadb-server -> hal-vault-mariadb. Controller at http://boundary.localhost:9200. NOTE: the plain `hal boundary mariadb enable` (without --with-vault) instead deploys a standalone hal-boundary-target-mariadb with a STATIC db user (admin/password) and no Vault brokering — only the --with-vault path tells the Vault-dynamic-credentials story. The lab wires a single DBA principal/role (no separate least-privilege 'regular user' role) and does not enable audit devices/session recording. statusTool returns TEXT status (no structured payload), so observable.linkFrom is null.

capabilities.label: Vault Secrets Operator on Kubernetes (native sync vs CSI)
capabilities.provides: Vault as the source of truth for application secrets on Kubernetes: the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) reconciles a Vault secret into a workload, either by syncing it to a native Kubernetes Secret (env var) or by projecting it through the CSI driver (mounted file) — the app never talks to Vault directly.
capabilities.manualTrigger: Native mode only: update the source secret in Vault (e.g. vault kv put kv-k8s/app1 <key>=<new-value>) and refresh the demo app — VSO re-syncs within refreshAfter (15s) and auto-rolls the pod.

observable.what: The demo app at http://web.localhost:8088 serves a value that originated in Vault and was delivered by VSO without the app calling Vault. In native mode, changing the value in Vault triggers a rolling restart (rolloutRestartTargets) of hal-web-backend; because hal-web-proxy fronts the backend (replicas 2, maxUnavailable 0, maxSurge 1) the reload is zero-downtime and transparent to the user. In CSI mode the value is projected as a mounted file with no native Kubernetes Secret and no auto-rollout.

capabilities.notes: Action `hal vault k8s enable` brings up a KinD cluster (on hal-net), installs the Vault Secrets Operator via Helm into namespace vso, wires Vault auth (kubernetes/ native, or jwt-k8s/ OIDC with --jwt), and deploys a demo app exposed at http://web.localhost:8088 (service hal-web-proxy in namespace app1, fronting Deployment hal-web-backend). Requires kind + kubectl + helm on PATH. statusTool get_k8s_integration_status runs `hal vault k8s` (status) and returns TEXT status (KinD/VSO/auth/demo-mode), so observable.linkFrom is null. TWO DELIVERY MODES on the same command: (1) NATIVE (default) — VaultStaticSecret (mount kv-k8s, path app1, refreshAfter 15s) writes a real Kubernetes Secret hal-web-secret consumed as an env var, with rolloutRestartTargets -> Deployment hal-web-backend so a Vault value change auto-rolls the pod. (2) CSI (--csi) — secret is projected via csi.vso.hashicorp.com directly into the pod's (tmpfs/memory) volume as a file; NO Kubernetes Secret is created and there is NO rolloutRestartTargets auto-rollout. ENTERPRISE GATE: --csi requires Vault Enterprise (isVaultEnterprise checks health.Version contains 'ent'; sets helm csi.enabled=true + CRD csisecrets.secrets.hashicorp.com). On Vault Community Edition, `--csi` is detected as unlicensed and SILENTLY DOWNGRADES to native sync (csiMode=false) — so the out-of-etcd CSI story is only available on Enterprise. SECURITY-TRADEOFF FRAMING (state precisely, do not overclaim): a native Kubernetes Secret is persisted in etcd base64-encoded and is only encrypted at rest if the cluster has etcd encryption-at-rest (KMS/aescbc) configured; it is visible via `kubectl get secret` under namespace RBAC, and env-var consumption can leak via process listings/crash dumps. CSI avoids this by NOT creating a persistent Secret object (file lives only in the pod's volume) — its advantage is 'not resident in etcd', NOT 'stronger encryption'. The auto-reload demo (refreshAfter + rolloutRestartTargets + transparent proxy) is NATIVE-ONLY; never promise it for CSI. The reverse trade is that CSI gives up that transparent auto-rollout.
